sections.name: Hook
lines: s_hook
Every photo on your phone is stored as electrons, trapped in tiny cages that hold them even with the power off.
s_title
Here's how flash memory works, in five steps.

sections.name: Billions of cells
lines: s_bits
Step one. A photo is just a long list of ones and zeros. Your phone keeps them in a chip called flash memory.
s_cells
It's packed with billions of tiny memory cells. A phone with two hundred and fifty six gigabytes holds about two trillion bits.

sections.name: Trapping electrons
lines: s_cage
Step two. Each cell has a little cage, called a floating gate, wrapped in insulation.
s_write
To store data, a jolt of voltage pushes electrons through the insulation, and into the cage.
s_keep
Once they're in, they're stuck. That's why your photos survive when the battery dies.

sections.name: Reading it back
lines: s_read
Step three. To read a cell, the chip checks how easily current flows past the cage. Trapped electrons make it harder, and that's a different value.
s_levels
Modern cells don't just hold one bit. By trapping different amounts of electrons, each cell can store three or four bits.

sections.name: Stacking up
lines: s_layers
Step four. To fit even more, the cells are stacked into towers, more than two hundred layers high, like a skyscraper on a chip.

sections.name: Wearing out
lines: s_wear
Step five. Every time a cell is erased and rewritten, its insulation wears a tiny bit.
s_level
So a controller chip spreads the writing around evenly, so no single cell wears out early. It's called wear levelling.
s_erase
Flash also erases in big blocks, not one cell at a time, so the controller shuffles data around behind the scenes.

sections.name: Recap
lines: w_recap
Photos are bits. Cells trap electrons. The amount of charge sets the value, the cells stack in layers, and the writing gets spread out evenly.
outro
So your memories really are made of electrons. Follow for more of the tech you use every day.
